content: Patients with long-term ulcerative colitis or colonic Crohn's disease are at a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer (CRC) compared to the general population. This review evaluated whether endoscopic surveillance could improve survival by enabling earlier detection of CRC or its precursor, dysplasia, in individuals with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The objective of this review was to determine the effectiveness of cancer surveillance programs in diagnosing IBD-associated CRC and reducing CRC-related mortality in patients with IBD. To achieve this, databases such as MEDLINE, EMBASE, CENTRAL, and clinicaltrials.gov were searched up to September 19, 2016. Additional studies were identified through conference abstracts and reference lists. The inclusion criteria required randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or observational studies (cohort or case-control) that evaluated any form of endoscopic surveillance for early CRC detection. Studies needed to include a comparison group without surveillance to be eligible. Two authors independently reviewed and extracted data from the studies, focusing on primary outcomes like CRC detection and secondary outcomes such as CRC-related death, time to cancer detection, time to death, and adverse events. Five observational studies involving 7,199 patients met the inclusion criteria. No RCTs were identified. The included studies were assessed for quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa scale, but all were deemed to have a high risk of bias due to their observational nature. Statistical heterogeneity was evaluated, and data were pooled using fixed-effects models when appropriate. Three studies were combined to compare CRC detection rates between surveillance and non-surveillance groups. The non-surveillance group had a significantly higher rate of CRC detection (3.17%) compared to the surveillance group (1.83%), with an odds ratio (OR) of 0.58 (95% CI 0.42 to 0.80; P = 0.0009). Four studies were pooled to assess CRC-related mortality. Patients in the surveillance group had a significantly lower death rate from CRC (8%) compared to those in the non-surveillance group (22%), with an OR of 0.36 (95% CI 0.19 to 0.69; P = 0.002). Two studies examined the stage of CRC at diagnosis. Early-stage CRC (Duke stages A & B) was more frequently detected in the surveillance group (16%) compared to the non-surveillance group (8%), with an OR of 5.40 (95% CI 1.51 to 19.30; P = 0.009). Conversely, late-stage CRC (Duke stages C & D) was more common in the non-surveillance group (16%) than in the surveillance group (9%), although this difference was not statistically significant (OR 0.46, 95% CI 0.08 to 2.51; P = 0.37). The quality of evidence for all outcomes was rated as very low using the GRADE criteria. Other pre-specified outcomes, such as time to cancer detection, time to death, and adverse events, were not reported in the included studies. In conclusion, the available data suggest that colonoscopic surveillance in patients with IBD may reduce the incidence of CRC and CRC-related mortality by facilitating earlier detection. The observed survival benefit may be partially explained by the higher detection rate of early-stage CRC in the surveillance group. However, the quality of evidence is very low, and ethical considerations make it unlikely that RCTs will be conducted to further evaluate the efficacy of endoscopic surveillance in this population.
